claim: Hedgehog signaling is critical for vertebrate central nervous system (CNS) development.
source: Hedgehog signaling is critical for vertebrate central nervous system (CNS) development, but its role in CNS biology in other organisms is poorly characterized.
evidence: This is a general statement about established knowledge in the field, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: The role of Hedgehog signaling in CNS biology in non-vertebrate organisms is poorly characterized.
source: Hedgehog signaling is critical for vertebrate central nervous system (CNS) development, but its role in CNS biology in other organisms is poorly characterized.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field based on literature review.

claim: In the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, hedgehog (hh) is expressed in medial cephalic ganglia neurons.
source: In the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, hedgehog (hh) is expressed in medial cephalic ganglia neurons, suggesting a possible role in CNS maintenance or regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B and cited literature.

claim: Expression of hh in medial cephalic ganglia neurons suggests a possible role in CNS maintenance or regeneration.
source: In the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, hedgehog (hh) is expressed in medial cephalic ganglia neurons, suggesting a possible role in CNS maintenance or regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the expression pattern observed.

claim: RNA sequencing of planarian brain tissue was performed following RNAi of hh and patched (ptc).
source: We performed RNA sequencing of planarian brain tissue following RNAi of hh and patched (ptc), which encodes the Hh receptor.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: patched (ptc) encodes the Hh receptor.
source: We performed RNA sequencing of planarian brain tissue following RNAi of hh and patched (ptc), which encodes the Hh receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hedgehog signaling pathway.

claim: Two misregulated genes, intermediate filament-1 (if-1) and calamari (cali), were identified from RNA sequencing.
source: Two misregulated genes, intermediate filament-1 (if-1) and calamari (cali), were expressed in a previously unidentified non-neural CNS cell type.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: if-1 and cali are expressed in a previously unidentified non-neural CNS cell type.
source: Two misregulated genes, intermediate filament-1 (if-1) and calamari (cali), were expressed in a previously unidentified non-neural CNS cell type.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data showing expression in cells that do not express neuronal markers (Figure 3).

claim: The if-1+/cali+ cells express orthologs of astrocyte-associated genes involved in neurotransmitter uptake and metabolism.
source: These cells expressed orthologs of astrocyte-associated genes involved in neurotransmitter uptake and metabolism, and extended processes enveloping regions of high synapse concentration.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data showing co-expression of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, and gat (Figure 3I-L).

claim: The if-1+/cali+ cells extend processes enveloping regions of high synapse concentration.
source: These cells expressed orthologs of astrocyte-associated genes involved in neurotransmitter uptake and metabolism, and extended processes enveloping regions of high synapse concentration.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing IF-1+ processes associated with Synapsin+ regions (Figure 4H-K).

claim: The if-1+/cali+ cells are proposed to be planarian glia.
source: We propose that these cells are planarian glia.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular markers, morphology, and localization data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Planarian glia are distributed broadly.
source: Planarian glia were distributed broadly, but only expressed if-1 and cali in the neuropil near hh+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data showing gs+, gat+, and other marker+ cells throughout the animal (Figure 3O-S).

claim: Planarian glia only express if-1 and cali in the neuropil near hh+ neurons.
source: Planarian glia were distributed broadly, but only expressed if-1 and cali in the neuropil near hh+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data showing if-1/cali expression adjacent to hh+ neurons (Figure 2D) and loss of expression upon hh RNAi (Figure 2H-I).

claim: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway has been implicated in numerous developmental processes across the Metazoa, including limb and midline development in vertebrates and segmentation in Drosophila.
source: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway has been implicated in numerous developmental processes across the Metazoa, including limb and midline development in vertebrates and segmentation in Drosophila (Ingham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ingham et al., 2011.

claim: Little is known about the role of Hh signaling in the Lophotrochozoa.
source: Little is known, however, about the role of Hh signaling in the Lophotrochozoa, one of the three superphyla that comprise the Bilateria.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Lophotrochozoa is one of the three superphyla that comprise the Bilateria.
source: Little is known, however, about the role of Hh signaling in the Lophotrochozoa, one of the three superphyla that comprise the Bilateria.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is a model system for the study of stem cell biology, wound response, and tissue patterning.
source: One member of the Lophotrochozoa, the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, is a model system for the study of stem cell biology, wound response, and tissue patterning (Reddien et al., 2005a; Sanchez Alvarado and Newmark, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reddien et al., 2005a and Sanchez Alvarado and Newmark, 1999.

claim: Planarians are free-living platyhelminthes capable of regenerating essentially any lost tissue.
source: Planarians are free-living platyhelminthes capable of regenerating essentially any lost tissue, a process involving the maintenance of a pluripotent stem cell population throughout adulthood (Morgan, 1898; Reddien, 2011; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Wagner et al., 2011; Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Morgan, 1898; Reddien, 2011; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Wagner et al., 2011; Witchley et al., 2013.

claim: Planarian regeneration involves the maintenance of a pluripotent stem cell population throughout adulthood.
source: Planarians are free-living platyhelminthes capable of regenerating essentially any lost tissue, a process involving the maintenance of a pluripotent stem cell population throughout adulthood (Morgan, 1898; Reddien, 2011; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Wagner et al., 2011; Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Morgan, 1898; Reddien, 2011; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Wagner et al., 2011; Witchley et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of Hh signaling in planarians perturbs regeneration of the anteroposterior (AP) axis.
source: Inhibition of Hh signaling in planarians perturbs regeneration of the anteroposterior (AP) axis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glazer et al., 2010; Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009.

claim: hh(RNAi) animals regenerate bifurcated or no tails.
source: hh(RNAi) animals regenerate bifurcated or no tails, whereas ptc(RNAi) animals regenerate anterior tails instead of heads (Glazer et al., 2010; Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glazer et al., 2010; Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009.

claim: ptc(RNAi) animals regenerate anterior tails instead of heads.
source: hh(RNAi) animals regenerate bifurcated or no tails, whereas ptc(RNAi) animals regenerate anterior tails instead of heads (Glazer et al., 2010; Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glazer et al., 2010; Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009.

claim: The planarian CNS consists of a pair of cephalic ganglia and ventral nerve cords.
source: The planarian CNS consists of a pair of cephalic ganglia and ventral nerve cords, each comprised of a cortex of neuronal cell bodies surrounding a neurite-filled neuropil (Morita and Best, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morita and Best, 1965.

claim: Each component of the planarian CNS is comprised of a cortex of neuronal cell bodies surrounding a neurite-filled neuropil.
source: The planarian CNS consists of a pair of cephalic ganglia and ventral nerve cords, each comprised of a cortex of neuronal cell bodies surrounding a neurite-filled neuropil (Morita and Best, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morita and Best, 1965.

claim: hh is expressed in cells along the medial domain of the cephalic ganglia.
source: hh is expressed in cells along the medial domain of the cephalic ganglia (Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009), a location analogous to the vertebrate neural tube floor plate (Dessaud et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009 and data in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The location of hh expression in planarians is analogous to the vertebrate neural tube floor plate.
source: hh is expressed in cells along the medial domain of the cephalic ganglia (Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009), a location analogous to the vertebrate neural tube floor plate (Dessaud et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on spatial comparison, supported by citation to Dessaud et al., 2008.

claim: Roles for Hh signaling in planarian nervous system regeneration have not been described.
source: However, roles for Hh signaling in planarian nervous system regeneration have not been described, despite a wealth of information on its involvement in the CNS of other systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The vertebrate ortholog Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is secreted from the floor plate and forms a ventral-to-dorsal morphogenetic gradient that establishes domains of transcription factor expression in the ventral neural tube.
source: The vertebrate ortholog Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is secreted from the floor plate and forms a ventral-to-dorsal morphogenetic gradient that establishes domains of transcription factor expression in the ventral neural tube (Dessaud et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dessaud et al., 2008.

claim: Each domain in the vertebrate neural tube generates a distinct complement of progenitors that differentiate into neurons and glia.
source: Each domain generates a distinct complement of progenitors that differentiate into neurons and glia (Dessaud et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dessaud et al., 2008.

claim: The Drosophila neurectoderm has a similar ventral-to-dorsal distribution of orthologous transcription factors to vertebrates.
source: The Drosophila neurectoderm has a similar ventral-to-dorsal distribution of orthologous transcription factors, but Hh signaling is not required to establish these domains (Cornell and Ohlen, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cornell and Ohlen, 2000.

claim: Hh signaling is not required to establish transcription factor domains in the Drosophila neurectoderm.
source: The Drosophila neurectoderm has a similar ventral-to-dorsal distribution of orthologous transcription factors, but Hh signaling is not required to establish these domains (Cornell and Ohlen, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cornell and Ohlen, 2000.

claim: Hh signaling has been implicated in specifying oligodendrocyte progenitors in the neural tube.
source: In addition to specifying oligodendrocyte progenitors in the neural tube (Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010), the pathway is also involved in inducing reactive astrogliosis in response to brain injury in adult mammals (Sirko et al., 2013), specifying subtypes of midline glia during Drosophila development (Watson et al., 2011), and regulating gene expression in astrocyte subtypes (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010.

claim: Hh signaling is involved in inducing reactive astrogliosis in response to brain injury in adult mammals.
source: In addition to specifying oligodendrocyte progenitors in the neural tube (Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010), the pathway is also involved in inducing reactive astrogliosis in response to brain injury in adult mammals (Sirko et al., 2013), specifying subtypes of midline glia during Drosophila development (Watson et al., 2011), and regulating gene expression in astrocyte subtypes (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sirko et al., 2013.

claim: Hh signaling is involved in specifying subtypes of midline glia during Drosophila development.
source: In addition to specifying oligodendrocyte progenitors in the neural tube (Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010), the pathway is also involved in inducing reactive astrogliosis in response to brain injury in adult mammals (Sirko et al., 2013), specifying subtypes of midline glia during Drosophila development (Watson et al., 2011), and regulating gene expression in astrocyte subtypes (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2011.

claim: Hh signaling is involved in regulating gene expression in astrocyte subtypes.
source: In addition to specifying oligodendrocyte progenitors in the neural tube (Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010), the pathway is also involved in inducing reactive astrogliosis in response to brain injury in adult mammals (Sirko et al., 2013), specifying subtypes of midline glia during Drosophila development (Watson et al., 2011), and regulating gene expression in astrocyte subtypes (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Farmer et al., 2016.

claim: Cells in the medial domain of the cephalic ganglion lobes express both pc2 and hh.
source: Cells in the medial domain of the cephalic ganglion lobes expressed both pc2 and hh (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some, but not all, hh+ cells express the cholinergic neuron marker chat.
source: The cholinergic neuron marker Smed-choline acetyltransferase (chat) (Nishimura et al., 2010) was also expressed in some, but not all, hh+ cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Nishimura et al., 2010.

claim: 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries.
source: Differential expression analysis of cephalic ganglia versus head fragments following control RNAi revealed that, of the total 15,113 transcripts passing our filters (see methods), 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched and 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries (adjusted p-value <0.05, log2 fold change >1.0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries.
source: Differential expression analysis of cephalic ganglia versus head fragments following control RNAi revealed that, of the total 15,113 transcripts passing our filters (see methods), 2237 transcripts were significantly enriched and 1938 transcripts were significantly diminished in cephalic ganglia libraries over head fragment libraries (adjusted p-value <0.05, log2 fold change >1.0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Broadly expressed neuronal markers syn, chat, and pc2 were only somewhat enriched in cephalic ganglia tissue.
source: Broadly expressed neuronal markers syn, chat, and pc2 were only somewhat enriched (Figure 1E), consistent with the fact that these genes are also expressed in the peripheral nervous system located throughout the head.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and inference about peripheral nervous system expression.

claim: Genes expressed in cells restricted to the medial CNS, such as hh and 1020HH, were more highly enriched at 57-fold and 81-fold, respectively.
source: Conversely, genes expressed in cells restricted to the medial CNS, such as hh and the prohormone-encoding gene 1020HH (Collins et al., 2010) were more highly enriched, at 57-fold and 81-fold, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Collins et al., 2010.

claim: Expression of hh in hh(RNAi) animals was significantly reduced.
source: Expression of hh in hh(RNAi) animals was, as expected, significantly reduced (padj <0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ptc expression was decreased in ptc(RNAi) animals as well as in hh(RNAi) animals.
source: ptc expression was decreased in ptc(RNAi) animals as well as in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hh acts by negatively regulating Patched protein, which in turn is a negative regulator of transcriptional targets of Hh signaling including the ptc gene itself.
source: Hh acts by negatively regulating Patched protein, which in turn is a negative regulator of transcriptional targets of Hh signaling including the ptc gene itself (Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varjosalo and Taipale, 2008.

claim: The Hh signaling pathway is required for establishing expression domains of the transcription factors Nk2.2, Nk6.1, and Pax6 in the developing vertebrate neural tube.
source: The Hh signaling pathway is required for establishing expression domains of the transcription factors Nk2.2, Nk6.1, and Pax6 in the developing vertebrate neural tube (Briscoe and Thérond, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Briscoe and Thérond, 2013.

claim: Absence of SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate results in loss of cell types that normally form in these domains.
source: Absence of SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate results in loss of cell types that normally form in these domains (Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruiz i Altaba et al., 2003.

claim: In intact planarians, Hh signaling does not modulate expression domains of orthologous transcription factors nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b.
source: By contrast, we were unable to find evidence that in intact planarians, which exhibit extensive tissue turnover and new cell type specification, Hh signaling modulates expression domains of orthologous transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1F) and FISH data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The expression levels of nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b were not significantly changed in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals versus controls.
source: The expression levels of Smed-nkx2 (nkx2), Smed-nkx6 (nkx6), and Smed-pax6b (pax6b) (Scimone et al., 2014a) were not significantly changed in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals versus controls (Figure 1F), and we confirmed this finding by FISH (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1F), FISH data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and citation to Scimone et al., 2014a.

claim: if-1 encodes a member of the cytoplasmic intermediate filament family.
source: if-1 encodes a member of the cytoplasmic intermediate filament family (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Intermediate filaments are cytoskeletal proteins that provide structural support and mechanical stress resistance in a variety of cell types.
source: Intermediate filaments are cytoskeletal proteins that provide structural support and mechanical stress resistance in a variety of cell types (Herrmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2007.

claim: cali encodes a predicted protein with some similarity to vertebrate protocadherin PCDH19 but lacks clear cadherin domains.
source: cali encodes a predicted protein with some similarity to vertebrate protocadherin PCDH19 but lacks clear cadherin domains (Frank and Kemler, 2002), and we therefore named this gene based on the morphology of the cells expressing it (see below).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to Frank and Kemler, 2002.

claim: if-1 and cali are co-expressed primarily in cells in the neuropil of both the cephalic ganglia and the ventral nerve cords.
source: FISH analysis revealed that if-1 and cali were co-expressed primarily in cells in the neuropil, the neurite-dense region surrounded by neuron cell bodies (Best and Noel, 1969; Morita and Best, 1965), of both the cephalic ganglia and the ventral nerve cords (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to Best and Noel, 1969; Morita and Best, 1965.

claim: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil express ptc.
source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil express ptc.
source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: if-1+/cali+ cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling.
source: 97.8% of if-1+/cali+ cells inside the neuropil and 100% of if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil expressed ptc, indicating that these cells are likely to be responsive to Hh signaling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on ptc expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: if-1+/cali+ neuropil cells are adjacent to the hh+ neurons in the medial cortex.
source: Additionally, if-1+/cali+ neuropil cells were adjacent to the hh+ neurons in the medial cortex, placing them in close proximity to a source of Hh ligand (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: if-1 and cali transcripts are detected in processes extending from the bodies of cells within the neuropil.
source: if-1 and cali transcripts were detected in processes extending from the bodies of cells within the neuropil of both the cephalic ganglia and ventral nerve cords, indicating an elaborate morphology for these cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Upon inhibition of hh, the density of if-1+/cali+ cells decreased both inside and outside the neuropil.
source: Upon hh RNAi, the density of if-1+/cali+ cells decreased both inside and outside the neuropil (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: The density of cells expressing either or both if-1 and cali in ptc(RNAi) animals increased slightly inside and considerably outside the neuropil.
source: Accordingly, the density of cells expressing either or both if-1 and cali in ptc(RNAi) animals increased slightly inside and considerably outside the neuropil (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: During regeneration, if-1+/cali+ cells accumulate in the blastema.
source: During regeneration, if-1+/cali+ cells accumulated in the blastema, the outgrowth that forms at wounds and replaces missing tissue.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No if-1+/cali+ cells are observed in the blastema in hh(RNAi) animals.
source: As expected, no if-1+/cali+ cells were observed in the blastema in hh(RNAi) animals.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ptc(RNAi) anterior blastemas have a large number of if-1+/cali+ cells despite impaired head formation.
source: Nonetheless, ptc(RNAi) anterior blastemas had a large number of if-1+/cali+ cells despite the impaired head formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inhibition of gli-1 results in loss of if-1 and cali signal.
source: RNAi of gli-1 resulted in loss of if-1 and cali signal whereas RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 did not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 does not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali.
source: RNAi of gli-1 resulted in loss of if-1 and cali signal whereas RNAi of gli-2 and gli-3 did not have any discernable effect on expression of if-1 and cali (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hh signaling is required for if-1 and cali expression to be detected in the neuropil.
source: We conclude that Hh signaling is required for if-1 and cali expression to be detected in the neuropil.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNAi experiments showing loss of if-1/cali expression upon hh and gli-1 inhibition.

claim: pc2, chat, and syn are not expressed in any if-1+/cali+ cells.
source: pc2, chat, and syn, three markers expressed broadly in planarian neurons, were not expressed in any if-1+/cali+ cells, raising the possibility that these cells are not neurons (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels, neurotransmitter synthesis enzymes, synaptic vesicle proteins, and neuronal transcription factors are not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
source: Genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels, a potassium channel, a sodium channel, a calcium channel, a sodium and potassium co-transporter, Glutamic acid decarboxylase (gd), Tyrosine hydroxylase (th), Tryptophan hydroxylase (tph), three Synaptotagmin family members, Synaptogyrin 2, synaptic vesicle fusion proteins SNAP25 and Unc-13, the vesicular neurotransmitter transporters VAchT and VGluT, and neuronal transcription factors were all not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3D–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3D-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: netrin-2 is not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
source: netrin-2, a marker previously described to be expressed in cells in the neuropil (Cebrià and Newmark, 2005), also was not expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citation to Cebrià and Newmark, 2005.

claim: if-1+/cali+ cells are not neurons.
source: We conclude that, despite localization within the CNS and the presence of cytoplasmic extensions, if-1+/cali+ cells are not neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of neuronal marker expression in if-1+/cali+ cells.

claim: gs is expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells in the ventral parenchyma and the intestine.
source: Smed-gs (gs) encodes an ortholog of Glutamine Synthetase and was expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells in the ventral parenchyma and the intestine (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3I and WISH data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: eaat2-1 and eaat2-2 are expressed in the majority of if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil and to a lesser degree outside the neuropil.
source: Two genes encoding orthologs of the glutamate transporter GLT-1/EAAT2 (Featherstone, 2011), Smed-eaat2-1 (eaat2-1) and Smed-eaat2-2 (eaat2-2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), were also expressed in the majority of if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil and to a lesser degree outside the neuropil (Figure 3J–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3J-K, phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and citation to Featherstone, 2011.

claim: gat is expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells.
source: Smed-gat (gat) is predicted to encode an ortholog of a family of GABA, creatine, and taurine transporters that are commonly used as invertebrate and vertebrate glia markers (Carducci et al., 2012; Featherstone, 2011; Minelli et al., 1996; Pow et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). gat was also expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3L, phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and citations to Carducci et al., 2012; Featherstone, 2011; Minelli et al., 1996; Pow et al., 2002.

claim: glut is co-expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells outside the neuropil.
source: We found a glucose transporter ortholog, Smed-glut (glut) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), co-expressed in if-1+/cali+ cells in the neuropil as well as in cells outside the neuropil (Figure 3M, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3M and phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: trpm is co-expressed with if-1 and cali in the neuropil, and expression is also observed in cells of the ventral parenchyma and pharynx.
source: The expression pattern of trpm was similar to that of gs and gat; trpm was co-expressed with if-1 and cali in the neuropil, and expression was also observed in cells of the ventral parenchyma and pharynx (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3N and phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: gs+ cells outside the cephalic ganglia express gat, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, glut, and trpm.
source: Indeed, we found that gs+ cells outside the cephalic ganglia expressed gat (Figure 3O), eaat2-1 (Figure 3P), eaat2-2 (Figure 3Q), glut (Figure 3R), and trpm (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3O-S.

claim: gs+ cells and glut+ cells outside the neuropil express ptc.
source: We found that gs+ cells and glut+ cells outside the neuropil also expressed ptc, suggesting that at least a subset of the cells are competent to respond to Hh signaling (Figure 3T,U).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3T-U.

claim: gs+ and eaat2-1+ cells outside the neuropil do not express pc2.
source: To ensure that these cells outside the neuropil were not neurons, we performed double FISH for pc2 with gs or eaat2-1 and found no evidence of co-expression (Figure 3V,W).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 3V-W.

claim: Co-expression of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, and gat indicates that these cells function to reuptake and metabolize neurotransmitters.
source: Co-expression of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, and gat indicates that these cells function to reuptake and metabolize neurotransmitters, a role performed in the vertebrate nervous system by astrocytes (Anderson and Swanson, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker co-expression and citation to Anderson and Swanson, 2000.

claim: The cells expressing glial markers are hypothesized to be glia.
source: Because these cells are embedded in the planarian nervous system and express glial markers rather than neuronal markers, we hypothesize that they are glia.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on molecular marker expression, localization, and morphology data.

claim: RNAi of gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, gat, glut, and trpm did not result in observable morphological or behavioral effects.
source: To determine the role of these glia markers in planarian biology, we performed RNAi on gs, eaat2-1, eaat2-2, gat, glut, and trpm. However, we did not observe any morphological or behavioral effects in these animals during normal tissue turnover in uninjured animals and following head and tail amputation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations following RNAi.

claim: IF-1+ cellular extensions form an extensive network concentrated in the neuropil and extending out of the CNS.
source: Whole-mount immunofluorescence revealed an extensive network of IF-1+ branches concentrated in the neuropil and extending out of the CNS (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: IF-1+ cellular extensions form hollow columns oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis.
source: The IF-1+ cellular extensions also formed hollow columns oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RNAi of if-1 results in complete loss of IF-1 antibody immunolabeling.
source: RNAi of if-1 resulted in complete loss of IF-1 antibody immunolabeling, confirming that labeling was specific (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IF-1+ processes emerging from the cephalic ganglion neuropil follow the same tracts as α-Tubulin+ axon bundles.
source: The IF-1+ processes emerging from the cephalic ganglion neuropil followed the same tracts as the α-Tubulin+ axon bundles (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IF-1+ processes are embedded within nerve bundles and do not appear to fully enclose the commissural axon fascicle.
source: The IF-1+ processes were embedded within the nerve bundles and did not appear to fully enclose the commissural axon fascicle.
evidence: This is an observation based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: IF-1+ processes weave through the synapse-dense cephalic ganglion neuropil.
source: Immunofluorescence with both the anti-IF-1 antibody and the anti-Synapsin antibody showed IF-1+ processes weaving through the synapse-dense cephalic ganglion neuropil (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: IF-1+ processes appear to encapsulate and invade Synapsin+ clusters throughout the VNCs and the Orthogon.
source: Moreover, IF-1+ processes appeared to encapsulate and invade Synapsin+ clusters throughout the VNCs and the Orthogon (Figure 4I–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Individual IF-1+ processes extend from one Synapsin+ cluster to another, indicating that single planarian glia can enwrap multiple targets.
source: Individual IF-1+ processes also extended from one Synapsin+ cluster to another, indicating that single planarian glia can enwrap multiple targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Inhibition of hh results in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal.
source: Inhibition of hh resulted in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal and no change in expression or localization of Synapsin protein, whereas inhibition of ptc caused an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Inhibition of ptc causes an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal.
source: Inhibition of hh resulted in complete ablation of IF-1 immunofluorescence signal and no change in expression or localization of Synapsin protein, whereas inhibition of ptc caused an increase in IF-1 protein presence in cellular processes observed throughout the animal (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes.
source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The percentage of orthogonal axon bundles associated with IF-1+ processes decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition.
source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The percentage of orthogonal axon bundles associated with IF-1+ processes increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition.
source: Normally 15.1% of orthogonal axon bundles are associated with IF-1+ processes, whereas the percentage decreased to 2.1% following hh inhibition and increased to 61.4% following ptc inhibition (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: IF-1 protein perdures after if-1 mRNA is lost in hh(RNAi) animals.
source: In hh(RNAi) animals we observed IF-1 protein by immunofluorescence despite the loss of detectable if-1 FISH signal throughout the neuropil, suggesting that hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia over the 12-day period during which we performed RNAi (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by combined FISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia.
source: In hh(RNAi) animals we observed IF-1 protein by immunofluorescence despite the loss of detectable if-1 FISH signal throughout the neuropil, suggesting that hh RNAi impacts if-1 and cali transcription in existing glia over the 12-day period during which we performed RNAi (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of IF-1 protein despite loss of if-1 mRNA.

claim: Expression of gs, gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 is still observed throughout the neuropil in hh(RNAi) animals and is indistinguishable from control animals.
source: Unlike the case for if-1 and cali, expression of the other glia markers was still observed throughout the neuropil and was indistinguishable from control animals.
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inhibition of ptc has no effect on the expression or localization of gs, gat, eaat2-1, or eaat2-2.
source: Similarly, inhibition of ptc had no effect on the expression or localization of gs, gat, eaat2-1, or eaat2-2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is no significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals.
source: We also did not observe a significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals, although the proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals.
source: We also did not observe a significant change in the total number of gat+ cells within the neuropil in hh(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) animals compared to control animals, although the proportion of the gat+ population that co-expressed if-1 and cali was reduced in hh(RNAi) animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A large number of gat+/if-1+/cali+ cells are detected outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals despite no significant overall increase in the number of gat+ cells.
source: Conversely, whereas a small proportion of gat+ glia outside the neuropil expressed if-1 and cali in control(RNAi) animals, a large number of gat+/if-1+/cali+ cells were detected outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals despite no significant overall increase in the number of gat+ cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: if-1 and cali are induced in planarian glia outside the neuropil when Hh signaling is activated by ptc inhibition.
source: Given that planarian glia outside the neuropil also expressed ptc, these data suggest that if-1 and cali were induced in these cells when Hh signaling was activated by ptc inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increase in if-1+/cali+ cells outside the neuropil in ptc(RNAi) animals.

claim: Anterior blastemas of control(RNAi) animals after six days of regeneration contain cells expressing planarian glia markers.
source: Anterior blastemas of control(RNAi) animals after six days of regeneration contained cells expressing planarian glia markers, both inside the forming neuropil and outside.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In hh(RNAi) animals, expression of if-1 and cali is eliminated in blastemas, but cells expressing gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 are observed throughout the blastema.
source: In hh(RNAi) animals, expression of if-1 and cali was eliminated, but cells expressing gat, eaat2-1, and eaat2-2 were observed throughout the blastema (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of glia markers in newly formed cells of the blastema suggests that the animal is capable of regenerating glia in the absence of Hh signaling.
source: The presence of these markers in newly formed cells of the blastema suggests that the animal is capable of regenerating glia in the absence of Hh signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of glia marker expression in hh(RNAi) blastemas.

claim: An increase in the number of if-1+/cali+ cells is observed in ptc(RNAi) animals despite irradiation.
source: By contrast, we observed an increase in the number of if-1+/cali+ cells in ptc(RNAi) animals despite irradiation (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data and quantification shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The ectopic if-1+/cali+ cells outside of the neuropil in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals have branches.
source: The ectopic if-1+/cali+ cells outside of the neuropil in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals had branches, indicating that ectopic expression occurred in existing cells with complex morphology (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil is similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals.
source: Furthermore, the total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil was similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals, but the proportion of glut+ cells that expressed if-1 and cali was higher following RNAi of ptc (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The proportion of glut+ cells that express if-1 and cali is higher in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals.
source: Furthermore, the total number of glut+ cells outside of the neuropil was similar in control(RNAi) and ptc(RNAi) irradiated animals, but the proportion of glut+ cells that expressed if-1 and cali was higher following RNAi of ptc (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ptc RNAi induces expression of if-1 and cali in existing glut+ cells.
source: This indicates that ptc RNAi induced expression of if-1 and cali in existing glut+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increase in if-1+/cali+/glut+ cells without an increase in total glut+ cells in irradiated ptc(RNAi) animals.

claim: Cells with ectopic if-1 and cali expression in ptc(RNAi) animals are likely mature planarian glia.
source: These observations indicate that cells with ectopic if-1 and cali expression in ptc(RNAi) animals are likely mature planarian glia, and support a model that Hh signaling normally induces expression of if-1 and cali in planarian glia dependent on their proximity to hh+ neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on irradiation experiments showing ectopic expression in existing cells.

claim: Hh signaling normally induces expression of if-1 and cali in planarian glia dependent on their proximity to hh+ neurons.
source: These observations indicate that cells with ectopic if-1 and cali expression in ptc(RNAi) animals are likely mature planarian glia, and support a model that Hh signaling normally induces expression of if-1 and cali in planarian glia dependent on their proximity to hh+ neurons.
evidence: This is a model supported by the spatial relationship between hh+ neurons and if-1+/cali+ glia, and the effects of Hh pathway perturbation.

claim: Previous electron microscopy studies identified candidate planarian glia based on localization and appearance but did not provide molecular evidence.
source: Previous electron microscopy studies had identified candidate planarian glia based on their localization and appearance but did not provide any molecular evidence for their identity (Golubev, 1988; Morita and Best, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Golubev, 1988 and Morita and Best, 1966.

claim: This study provides the first molecular and morphological evidence for neuronal support cells in planarians.
source: We have described here the first molecular and morphological evidence for neuronal support cells in planarians.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ability of Hh signaling to modulate function in glia has been described in vertebrates.
source: The ability of Hh signaling to modulate function in glia has been described in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on reactive astrogliosis and astrocyte regulation.

claim: In reactive astrogliosis, SHH is one of the inductive signals that induces expression of the intermediate filament GFAP.
source: In reactive astrogliosis, the mammalian CNS response to injury, SHH is one of the inductive signals that induces expression of the intermediate filament GFAP (Sirko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sirko et al., 2013.

claim: Increased levels of GFAP protein result in an increase in cell size, which is necessary for the formation of an astrocytic scar at the wound site.
source: Increased levels of GFAP protein result in an increase in cell size, which is necessary for the formation of an astrocytic scar at the wound site (Wilhelmsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilhelmsson et al., 2004.

claim: The regulation of intermediate filament proteins by Hh signaling in glia is a commonality between planarians and vertebrates.
source: Although the function of this regulation has differences, the regulation of intermediate filament proteins by Hh signaling in glia is another striking commonality between planarians and vertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of findings in planarians with vertebrate literature.

claim: SHH secreted from neurons regulates distinct subpopulations of mammalian astrocytes.
source: Additionally, SHH secreted from neurons has been reported to regulate distinct subpopulations of mammalian astrocytes (Farmer et al., 2016; Garcia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Farmer et al., 2016 and Garcia et al., 2010.

claim: The ability for neurons to instruct astrocyte expression profiles in mammals is a similar feature to what is observed in planarians.
source: Although the genes regulated by Hh signaling in these glial populations is different, the ability for neurons to instruct astrocyte expression profiles in mammals is a strikingly similar feature to what we observe in planarians (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of findings in planarians with mammalian literature, supported by citation to Farmer et al., 2016.

claim: SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate establishes distinct domains of transcription factor expression in the ventral neural tube.
source: SHH expression in the vertebrate floor plate establishes distinct domains of transcription factor expression in the ventral neural tube.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate neural development.

claim: These domains in the vertebrate neural tube first give rise to neurons and then, at later stages of development, glia.
source: These domains first give rise to neurons and then, at later stages of development, glia (Dessaud et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dessaud et al., 2008 and Yu et al., 2013.

claim: The dorsal-ventral distribution of transcription factors in the developing CNS of Drosophila and Platynereis dumerilii resembles the distribution of orthologous transcription factors in the vertebrate neural tube.
source: The dorsal-ventral distribution of transcription factors in the developing CNS of Drosophila and the Lophotrochozoan Platynereis dumerilii bear a resemblance to the distribution of orthologous transcription factors in the vertebrate neural tube (Cornell and Ohlen, 2000; Denes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cornell and Ohlen, 2000 and Denes et al., 2007.

claim: Hh appears to play a role in the anterior-posterior patterning of Drosophila neuroblasts rather than dorsal-ventral patterning.
source: Hh, however, appears to play a role in the anterior-posterior patterning of Drosophila neuroblasts rather than dorsal-ventral patterning (Bhat, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhat, 1999.

claim: In Platynereis, a role for Hh in segment patterning has been identified, but no effect of pathway perturbation on the dorsal-ventral arrangement of CNS progenitor domains was described.
source: Similarly, in Platynereis, a role for Hh in segment patterning has been identified, but no effect of pathway perturbation on the dorsal-ventral (medial-lateral) arrangement of CNS progenitor domains was described (Denes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denes et al., 2007.

claim: Regionalized expression of orthologs of Hh-responsive vertebrate neural tube transcription factors appears unaffected by Hh signaling in uninjured planarians.
source: Here, we also find that regionalized expression in the cephalic ganglia of several orthologs of Hh-responsive vertebrate neural tube transcription factors appear unaffected by Hh signaling in uninjured planarians.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and FISH data showing no change in nkx2, nkx6, and pax6b expression.

claim: Hh signaling may have been co-opted into a dorsal-ventral patterning role in the nervous system in the deuterostome lineage.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that Hh signaling was co-opted into a dorsal-ventral patterning role in the nervous system in the deuterostome lineage.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparative analysis across phyla.

claim: The floor plate serves as a mediator of axonal midline crossing through the secretion of axon guidance cues.
source: The floor plate, which is induced by SHH secreted from the notochord, serves as a mediator of axonal midline crossing through the secretion of axon guidance cues (Colamarino and Tessier-Lavigne, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colamarino and Tessier-Lavigne, 1995.

claim: SHH acts as a chemoattractant and mediates cellular responses to other guidance cues.
source: SHH continues its involvement in neural patterning by acting as a chemoattractant and by mediating cellular responses to other guidance cues (Parra and Zou, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parra and Zou, 2010.

claim: The Drosophila midline glia are considered to be an analogous structure to the vertebrate floor plate.
source: The Drosophila midline glia are considered to be an analogous structure to the vertebrate floor plate because of similar gene expression and roles in controlling midline crossing (Evans and Bashaw, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Evans and Bashaw, 2010.

claim: Hh in Drosophila is required for the decision to form posterior midline glia instead of anterior midline glia.
source: Hh in Drosophila is required for the decision to form posterior midline glia, the function for which is still not fully understood, instead of anterior midline glia, which develop into ensheathing glia in the Drosophila neuropil (Watson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watson et al., 2011.

claim: A shared function of Hh signaling among Deuterostomes, Ecdysozoans, and Lophotrochozoans is in the control of glia near the midline.
source: A shared function of Hh signaling among Deuterostomes, Ecdysozoans, and Lophotrochozoans therefore appears to be in the control of glia near the midline.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of Hh signaling roles across phyla.

claim: Planarians are an ideal model for the study of regeneration.
source: Planarians are an ideal model for the study of regeneration because of their nearly unrivaled regenerative ability, their ease of culture, and the molecular tools developed for rapid study of gene function.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the planarian model system.

claim: The role of glia in regeneration has been investigated in vertebrates and insects.
source: The role of glia in regeneration has been investigated in vertebrates, where glia proliferate in response to brain injury, and in insects, where surface glia can reform the blood-brain barrier (Sofroniew, 2009; Treherne et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sofroniew, 2009 and Treherne et al., 1984.

claim: Astrocytic scars appear to counteract neural regeneration by blocking the extension of axons into the damaged region.
source: Interestingly, astrocytic scars appear to counteract neural regeneration by blocking the extension of axons into the damaged region (Silver and Miller, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silver and Miller, 2004.

claim: IF-1+ processes are not seen deviating from axonal tracts.
source: Several lines of evidence support the second hypothesis: IF-1+ processes are not seen deviating from axonal tracts and perturbations affecting gene regulation in planarian glia do not result in observable disruption to the neural network.
evidence: This is an observation based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: Perturbations affecting gene regulation in planarian glia do not result in observable disruption to the neural network.
source: Several lines of evidence support the second hypothesis: IF-1+ processes are not seen deviating from axonal tracts and perturbations affecting gene regulation in planarian glia do not result in observable disruption to the neural network.
evidence: This is based on observations following RNAi of Hh pathway components.

claim: A role for Hh signaling in CNS glia is a common feature across all three superphyla of the Bilateria.
source: Our data indicate that a role for Hh signaling in regulation of CNS glia is a common feature across all three superphyla of the Bilateria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative analysis of Hh signaling roles in glia across phyla.
